findings.reason: The protected Python solution computes the length of the longest good palindromic subsequence using 2D/3D dynamic programming over intervals and outer character states. It maintains rolling DP layers (length_minus_two and length_minus_one) tracking maximum lengths for each boundary character (0..25). When s[left] == s[right], it transitions by taking 2 + max(length_minus_two[left+1][letter] for letter != outer). The solution runs in O(n^2) time and O(n) space; no candidate is required.
Interval DP tracking boundary letters guarantees even-length palindromes with distinct adjacent letters everywhere except at the center.

Evaluating O(n^2) intervals over 26 boundary letters takes O(26 * n^2) = O(n^2) time. Rolling layers for length - 1 and length - 2 require O(26 * n) = O(n) auxiliary space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts string s and returns the maximum integer length of a good palindromic subsequence.

The approach accurately details boundary-letter interval DP, non-matching outer letter wrapping rules, rolling DP layer space optimizations, and O(n^2) time / O(n) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover memoized search recursion costs, 3D interval table space requirements, standard LPS DP boundary letter loss pitfalls, no-repeated-character zero outputs, all-equal-character length 2 caps, and non-contiguous subsequence ordering.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical rolling interval DP with 26-character boundary tracking algorithm with SHA-256 digests 8aa1ad25efb41cbce7966dafbba0da0f90eb69ca69f99723f4cdd52e277b3374 and 1bf868e978eb880fdb5ebbef02df05b16cd348411cc622e10d51d67c49201bea.
